items.title: JWST studies a tiny, metal-poor galaxy with just a fraction of the sun's oxygen abundance
items.summary: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have studied one of the most metal-poor galaxies known. items.title: Wave-like displays in animal groups may have evolved to deceive predators
items.summary: Some of the most striking patterns in collective behavior emerge in the face of danger. When a predator approaches, some animal groups morph into a vision of pulsing waves. These patterns might be more than a side effect of group living; they could have evolved as a form of deception, argue Dr. Edua

items.title: Runaway pulsar escapes the remnant of its own supernova
items.summary: A team of astronomers has spotted a rare example of a pulsar that has escaped the cloud of debris left by the supernova explosion in which it formed. Led by Rohit Dokara, formerly at the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy, the team made the discovery by chance, adding to just a handful of simi

items.title: 5G interference can alter high-impact weather forecasts
items.summary: Could leaks from future 5G networks interfere with satellite weather measurements and potentially alter forecasts? That's the concern of a group of researchers from the U.S. states of New Jersey and Maryland, with lead author Behzad Golparvar from Rutgers University in New Jersey.

items.title: Thailand tests find high lead, arsenic in river shellfish
items.summary: Thai authorities have found dangerous levels of arsenic and lead in shellfish and other species in rivers contaminated by suspected mining pollution from neighboring Myanmar, an official said Thursday.

items.title: FOTO Drevna egipatska građevina otkrivena iz svemira
items.summary: ARHEOLOZI su pomoću satelitskih snimki i tomografije otkrili 2600 godina staru građevinu u drevnom gradu Butu. Otkriće pruža nove spoznaje o građevinskim tehnikama starog Egipta.

items.title: Spain races to stop oil spill after ship capsizes off Ibiza
items.summary: Spanish authorities raced to contain any damage to ecologically valuable Mediterranean waters on Thursday after a tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes (7,700 tons) of diesel capsized off Ibiza, leaving one dead.

items.title: God-faced rings may have identified Mesoamerica's long-distance merchants
items.summary: Over 1,000 years ago, a Mesoamerican may have been traveling through foreign lands. Upon arriving at his destination, he held up his hand, adorned with a ring showing the face of a god, but what was this ring's purpose?

items.title: Global maritime trade set for zero growth in 2026: UN
items.summary: Global maritime trade—which carries more than 80% of the world's goods—is set to stagnate in 2026 due to shipping disruptions and trade uncertainties arising from the war in the Middle East, the United Nations said Thursday.

items.title: Protein redesign boosts DNA insertion activity and reveals how molecular machinery selects targets
items.summary: Genome engineering is exciting, given its vast potential to treat and even cure diseases, but it is still a largely uncharted biomedical innovation. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital recently uncovered the mechanisms involved in precisely integrating DNA into a target genomic

items.title: Do all groups drift toward rule by the few? Not when time is on their side
items.summary: For more than a century, a bleak idea has hung over the ideal of democracy: Given enough time, every group ends up ruled by a few. The idea, known as the iron law of oligarchy, was first proposed by the sociologist Robert Michels in the early 1900s.

items.title: Learning facts out of interest may take less mental effort than learning them for money
items.summary: When completing tasks or acquiring information, humans can be driven by intrinsic and extrinsic motivations. items.title: Two mechanisms of amino acid transport in a rare disease-associated protein revealed
items.summary: Cells must constantly exchange amino acids with their environment to make proteins and support numerous bodily processes. To do this, they have specialized transporters located in their membranes.

items.title: Scientists discover quasar formed within a mere 630 million years of the Big Bang, setting a record
items.summary: Scientists have discovered the most distant quasar yet, the core of a galaxy with a slow-chomping black hole at its center dating back to nearly the dawn of the universe.

items.title: Early Stone Age rock carvings in Scandinavia may have been signposts for hunting grounds
items.summary: Between roughly 9,000 and 4,000 B.C., artists in ancient Scandinavia painstakingly carved large, sometimes life-size images of elk, reindeer, bears and other creatures into rock faces teetering on the edge of fjords, rivers and lakes. But their meaning has long been debated.

items.title: Sensory deterrents aren't a 'one-size-fits-all' solution for sharks and rays
items.summary: A study on how select species of rays and sharks respond to sensory deterrents has reinforced why there isn't a one-size-fits-all solution to prevent fisheries bycatch.

items.title: Many buyers willing to pay more to know where their food comes from
items.summary: New research from Curtin University reveals many Australians are prepared to pay more for food when they know where it comes from and how animals are treated, despite ongoing cost-of-living pressures.

items.title: Mathematics fact fluency interventions for students with mathematics difficulties
items.summary: Associate professor Jonté Myers knows that developing fluency with mathematics facts is key to mathematics proficiency. However, many students struggle to develop these foundational skills.

items.title: Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease
items.summary: A combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin produced results comparable to antibiotics when used alongside standard treatment for severe gum disease, with benefits persisting long after supplementation ended. items.title: Loneliness is making us sick, but we may be treating it all wrong
items.summary: Loneliness can be surprisingly deadly, with previous research linking it to a roughly 30% increase in the risk of premature death. items.title: The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men
items.summary: Men and women appear to be similarly capable of multitasking, but men are more than twice as likely to ignore conversation while juggling multiple activities. Researchers believe this unexpected difference may help explain why women are widely perceived as better multitaskers.

items.title: Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds
items.summary: Scientists have solved the mystery of strange trenches scattered across Australia’s vast Nullarbor Plain, revealing an extensive hidden world beneath the surface. items.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
items.summary: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery

items.title: 'King tide' waves batter California coast, soaking San Francisco
items.summary: Massive waves carried on king tides battered California's coast Wednesday, prompting evacuations and soaking San Francisco, but sparing feared mass disruptions to Thanksgiving holiday travel.

items.title: Wildfires raze homes, displace wildlife on Australian island
items.summary: Wildfires have forced road closures, displaced animals and razed homes while engulfing over 10% of Australia's southeastern Flinders Island, emergency services said Thursday.

items.title: Some miniature Cas12m proteins can cut DNA after all
items.summary: An international research group led by graduate student Hayato Morinaga, Assistant Professor Satoshi N. Omura and Professor Osamu Nureki from the University of Tokyo has demonstrated for the first time that some Cas12m proteins do have an active state capable of cutting, or "cleaving," DNA. The team

items.title: FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical
items.summary: The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-held, lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

items.title: Dragonflies feast on other insects during autumn migrations
items.summary: Dragonflies feast on a host of insects—and each other—during their autumn migrations, new research shows. Scientists studied dragonflies at the Pass of Bujaruelo—a 30-meter (98-foot) gap between two high peaks in the Pyrenees, through which millions of insects migrate every year.

items.title: Seeking Refuge on Resolution Island
items.summary: New Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.

items.title: World's fastest animal could nearly double its livable territory by 2080 in the UK due to climate change
items.summary: Global warming and climate change could have the unexpected bounty of making Great Britain a more welcoming home for the fastest animal on Earth. The area suitable for peregrine falcons within the UK could grow by 74% by the year 2080 under a high-emissions climate scenario, a new study has shown.

items.title: Sending an Australian astronaut to space is expensive. How do we work out if it's worth it?
items.summary: Australia is currently in talks with the European Space Agency (ESA) over potentially flying Katherine Bennell-Pegg on a future space mission. items.title: Too much of this common nutrient could be accelerating blood vessel aging
items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a kidney protein that may hold an important key to vascular aging and longevity. items.title: New eyes in the sky make timber harvesting and forest conservation easier and more efficient
items.summary: Flying thousands of feet above northern and eastern Maine, Dave Sandilands searched for illegally dumped trash. items.title: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
items.summary: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. items.title: World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results
items.summary: Robot-assisted knee replacement surgery offers greater surgical precision, but a landmark clinical trial has revealed a surprising limitation. items.title: Dinosaurs likely tore meat like birds of prey
items.summary: Meat-eating dinosaurs probably fed by dragging their teeth backward through flesh like a saw rather than biting straight down like a dagger, new experiments suggest.

items.title: Disliking AI doesn't deter its influence
items.summary: An aversion to artificial intelligence (AI) does not lessen the influence of the technology on people and their decision-making, according to new research from City St George's, University of London.

items.title: Sweden tops global media freedom support rankings as international funding declines
items.summary: Sweden has been ranked the world's leading supporter of international media freedom, according to a new index. The index also highlights a decline in funding from 30 leading donor countries, despite growing threats to independent journalism worldwide.

items.title: Giant deer bones may push human arrival in Ireland back by 1,000 years
items.summary: A team of archaeologists and scientists has uncovered tantalizing new evidence that Late Upper Paleolithic hunter-gatherers may have lived in southern Ireland around 13,500 years ago—nearly a millennium earlier than currently confirmed.

items.title: Fermented milk may have held ritual power in Neolithic Denmark
items.summary: Experimental archaeology sheds light on the substances fermented in Neolithic Scandinavian pottery and deposited in tombs, suggesting fermented dairy products held symbolic significance in prehistoric funerary rituals.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in how the body burns calories
items.summary: Researchers have discovered that a drug can significantly increase the body's energy expenditure without clearly activating calorie-burning brown fat. The unexpected finding reveals a new challenge in developing obesity treatments that harness the body's natural fat-burning machinery.

items.title: Minecraft-like DNA cubes self-assemble into complex 3D nanostructures
items.summary: Associate professor Petr Sulc and his research team have developed a programmable DNA-based building system that could open new possibilities for nanorobots, three-dimensional electronics and next-generation nanotechnology.

items.title: Artificial photosynthesis uses waste CO₂ to grow protein-rich edible fungus in seven days
items.summary: While many people think first of meat when they think about dietary protein, most protein ultimately depends on plants, since livestock feed on grass, hay and other plants. items.title: Draining peatlands leaves a long legacy of warming
items.summary: Peatland ecosystems like bogs and swamps perform an important balancing act: Their vegetation takes up huge amounts of carbon dioxide, while their soil microbes produce methane. items.title: Stabilizing atomically thin metals with sandwich structures: Machine learning expands the search
items.summary: Atomically thin metals, metallenes, are promising materials for catalysis, electronics and energy conversion, but their synthesis has been challenging. items.title: Smartphone app uses AI to identify illegal wildlife products
items.summary: Illegal and unsustainable wildlife trade is a major driver of biodiversity loss. Thousands of animal species are traded, along with products made from them, ranging from ivory to scales and powders.

items.title: Certain fungi turn specialized plant cells into water-carrying cells using one protein
items.summary: Can a pathogen that causes damage to a plant also make that plant more resilient to drought? An international research team led by the University of Göttingen has investigated this apparent paradox. items.title: NASA namjerno zabila svemirsku letjelicu u asteroid. Nastao krater veličine stadiona
items.summary: VELIKA oštećenja nastala su 2022. godine, kada se NASA-ina letjelica sudarila s asteroidom Dimorphos.

items.title: Carbon nanotube measurements reveal quantum model better explains collective electron behavior
items.summary: An international team of scientists from Lithuania, Finland and Israel has conducted both theoretical and experimental research into carbon nanotubes, becoming the first to demonstrate which physical model governs the motion and interactions of electrons within them.

items.title: New inhibitor restores antibiotic activity against drug-resistant bacteria
items.summary: Researchers from Imperial College London and collaborators have identified a potent small-molecule inhibitor that can restore the activity of the antibiotic ciprofloxacin against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

items.title: NASA's Europa Clipper zooming by Earth on way to Jupiter's icy moon
items.summary: NASA's Europa Clipper will soon swing past Earth before making a yearslong beeline for Jupiter, where the orbiter will probe whether the ocean beneath its moon Europa's icy shell has the ingredients for life. The flyby will offer a propellant-saving boost and an opportunity to prepare for

items.title: Shopping as a 'collector' makes us want to buy more, new research shows
items.summary: Shoppers are more likely to buy products and pay more for them when they adopt a "collecting mindset," according to new research co-authored by Bayes Business School (City St George's, University of London).

items.summary: Massive stars often form in dense regions, called "hubs," where filamentary structures made of star-forming materials meet. These star-forming complexes are "hub-filament" systems.
